note: Printed speeds of the paces of manoeuvre. The sources disagree; each is a selectable basis (AnimSystem option gaitBasis). The default stays modern_range until the owner decides (PENDING OWNER).
mapping: manual walk -> clip walk; manual trot -> clip trot; manual gallop -> clip canter (nearest clip speed); a speed above gallop x gallopMargin -> clip gallop (full-speed charge, no printed speed)

sources.work: Wheeler, Joseph. A Revised System of Cavalry Tactics for the Use of the Cavalry and Mounted Infantry, C.S.A. Mobile: S. H. Goetzel & Co., 1863.

items.ref: Basis of Instruction, "Practice of Paces for Manoeuvre", p. 87
items.passage: walk 3 3/4 miles an hour, trot 7 1/2 miles an hour, gallop 10 miles an hour; a half mile to be walked in 8 minutes, trotted in 4, galloped in 3

items.ref: Squadron, Mounted, para 333 "To regulate the rapidity of the gaits", p. 177
items.passage: the mile at a walk in sixteen minutes, at a trot in eight, at the gallop in six

sources.note: a Confederate manual of 1863 (the cavalry of the Army of Tennessee); paras 333 and the Basis of Instruction agree (3.75 / 7.5 / 10 mph)

sources.work: Cooper's Cavalry Tactics, for the Use of Volunteers; to which is added a Manual for Colt's Revolver. New Orleans and Jackson, Miss.: 1861 (Confederate publication of the Cooke system).

items.passage: the walk three and a half to four miles an hour, the trot eight miles and a half an hour, the gallop eleven miles an hour (OCR reads "three and a h ilf")

sources.note: the same page says the gallop is not considered applicable to general manoeuvre, and that the pace is reckoned at one yard

sources.work: Instruction for Field Artillery. Prepared by a Board of Artillery Officers. Washington: Government Printing Office, 1863 (War Department order of March 1, 1863).
sources.archive: archive.org/details/cu31924030759330 (acquired copy; cross-checked in instructionforf01deptgoog, whose pagination differs: pp. 28 and 31)

items.ref: Pointing and Ranges, p. 42 (para on the charge of cavalry against a battery)

yards_per_phase.gait: round trot ("a little more than two minutes")

items.passage: cavalry 1,000 yards from the battery: first 400 yards at a walk approaching a gentle trot in about four and a half minutes; next 400 at a round trot in a little more than two minutes; last 200 at a gallop in about half a minute; about seven minutes in all

items.ref: Management of a Battery, Art. Fourth, p. 47
items.passage: A horse travels the distance of 400 yards at a walk in 4 1/2 minutes; at a trot in 2 minutes; at a gallop in 1 minute

sources.note: the one statement at p. 47 gives the three paces as horse speeds; p. 42 is an estimate of an enemy charge (rounded times)

sources.work: Cavalry Tactics (United States War Department, Second Part, School of the Trooper, of the Platoon and of the Squadron, Mounted), Washington: J. and G. S. Gideon, 1841 (superseded by Cooke's system, War Department notice 1 Nov 1861).

items.ref: para 600 "To regulate the rapidity of the gaits", p. 196
items.passage: at the walk from 100 to 110 paces per minute, at the trot from 200 to 230 per minute; the figure for the gallop is cut off in the OCR ("about 300")

sources.note: an older edition (OCR damaged); NOT used as a basis, kept as corroboration of the Wheeler and Cooper walk and trot (paces taken as yards after Cooper p. 7)

modern_range.label: modern equestrian ranges (the behaviour before this module)

wheeler_1863.label: Wheeler, Revised System of Cavalry Tactics, C.S.A., 1863

cooper_1861.label: Cooper's Cavalry Tactics, 1861 (walk taken at the middle of 3.5 to 4 mph)

fa_1863.label: Instruction for Field Artillery, 1863 (horse: 400 yd in 4.5 / 2 / 1 minute)

charge_schedule.note: the pace of the charge ("quicken the gallop to nearly full speed", para 189) has no printed speed; the horses must not be fatigued, "it should be as short as possible" (p. 210)
